subject: Biology
title: Sexual Dimorphism
description: A short lesson to help you apply Sexual Dimorphism.

hook.text: Male elephant seals weigh 10 times more than females. Male peacocks carry tails that slow them down. Why?

buildup.text: Sexual dimorphism—differences between sexes—evolves when males compete for access to females.

discovery.text: Larger males win fights for mates. More ornamented males are chosen by females. Both traits get amplified.

twist.text: In seahorses and pipefish, males are choosier—and females are the ones with flashy colors.

climax.text: The sex that invests less in offspring usually competes more. Investment determines who's picky.

punchline.text: Who competes and who chooses depends on who invests more.

quiz.question: In seahorses, which sex is more ornamented and competitive?

details.summary: Sexual dimorphism refers to physical differences between males and females of a species beyond reproductive organs. Driven by sexual selection, it produces features like the peacock's tail, deer antlers, and gorilla size difference that enhance mating success rather than survival.
details.whyItMatters: Sexual dimorphism demonstrates that evolution can favor traits harmful to survival if they increase reproductive success. Understanding how and why sexes differ illuminates the power of sexual selection as an evolutionary force.
takeaways: The peacock's tail evolved through female mate choice for elaborate displays
Male-male competition drives evolution of weapons like antlers and tusks
Extreme dimorphism often indicates a polygynous mating system

faq.question: Why does the peacock have such an impractical tail?
faq.answer: Female peahens prefer males with larger, more elaborate tails as honest signals of genetic quality. Only healthy males can afford the metabolic cost and predation risk of a huge tail. The tail handicap actually signals good genes to choosy females.

faq.question: Why are males usually more ornamented than females?
faq.answer: In most species, females invest more in offspring through eggs and parental care, making them the choosier sex. Males compete for female attention through ornaments and displays. The sex that invests less in offspring typically competes more for access to mates.
